subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: The storm knocked out the lights on the morning of the district race, and the school hall in Kanpur echoed with wind. Zeenat sat on the wet steps with her shoes untied, her hands shaking. Her friend Dilnaz crouched next to her. “I'm scared,” said Zeenat. “I know,” said Dilnaz. “You're nervous. That's okay. But you can do it. Try to run the first bend slowly and speed up when you see the flag.” Zeenat took a breath. “Okay.” Dilnaz tied her shoe. “You can do it,” she said again. Zeenat stood up, and they walked out together to the track.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz tie?
qa.a: Zeenat's shoe.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling on the steps, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt scared and nervous about the race, shown by her shaking hands and her saying “I'm scared.”

qa.q: What made Dilnaz's encouragement helpful?
qa.a: She did not deny the nervousness, said it was okay, and gave a concrete suggestion about running the first bend slowly.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel about her friend's race?
qa.a: She probably cares and wants to give belief and help, and she may also feel a little nervous herself. 🙂

grounding: A child says you can do it before a race, acknowledges nervousness and gives a concrete suggestion.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: “You can do it, Jahnavi!” said Akash, tapping her desk before the spelling test. “I can't,” she said, her fingers cold. “What if I forget?” Akash didn't tell her to stop worrying. He said, “Everybody gets nervous. Look at the words once, then read them slowly as you write.” Jahnavi nodded and took a long breath. “Okay. Slowly.” He gave her a small thumbs-up and went to his seat. During the test she wrote each word as slowly as she could. Later she told Akash, “I was still nervous, but the slow part helped.” He grinned.

qa.q: What test was Jahnavi about to take?
qa.a: A spelling test.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say she couldn't do it?
qa.a: She was nervous and worried she would forget the words, which is why her fingers were cold.

qa.q: What made Akash's encouragement more than a slogan?
qa.a: He said everyone gets nervous and gave a concrete tip to look at the words once and read slowly.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Jahnavi thanked him?
qa.a: He was probably happy that his help mattered, since he grinned.

grounding: A child says you can do it before a test, does not deny nervousness and gives a concrete suggestion.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: “I can't do it, Tanvir. My legs feel like noodles.” Sabina stood at the edge of the pool, shivering. “You're nervous. That's normal. I'm always nervous before a race.” “You are?” “Every time. My stomach does flips.” Sabina almost smiled. “So what do you do?” “I look at the far wall and only think about the first three strokes. Not the whole race. Just three.” “Three strokes.” “And you've swum this length a hundred times in practice. You can do it.” The whistle blew. Sabina looked at the far wall. One, two, three. Then she didn't stop until she touched it.

qa.q: What does Tanvir look at before a race?
qa.a: Tanvir looks at the far wall.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling at the edge of the pool?
qa.a: Sabina felt nervous and shaky, her legs like noodles.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's encouragement help more than just “You can do it”?
qa.a: He accepted her nervousness, shared his own and gave a concrete tip: focus on the first three strokes.

qa.q: What would change if Tanvir had said “Don't be silly, you're not nervous”?
qa.a: Sabina might have felt unheard and more anxious, with no plan to calm herself.

grounding: Shows a child encouraging a friend before a race without denying her nerves, and pairing belief with a concrete suggestion.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: I'm Zainab. Last year, before the maths olympiad, my friend Lokesh sat on the school steps looking grey. I said, “Don't worry! You'll be fine! You're a genius!” He looked even greyer. “You don't know that.” I felt useless. Then I remembered what my sister did for me before my dance exam: she didn't say I'd be fine; she said, “Your hands are cold. Warm them, then do the first move slowly.” So I tried again. “You're nervous, and that makes sense. Want to go over the three formulas you always forget, just once?” We did. His colour came back a bit. He came third. I learned that encouraging needs a plan, not just cheering.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh finish in the olympiad?
qa.a: Lokesh came third.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling on the school steps?
qa.a: Lokesh was nervous and anxious before the olympiad, looking grey.

qa.q: What did Zainab change the second time, and why did it work?
qa.a: Zainab accepted his nerves and offered a concrete step, going over the three formulas he always forgets.

qa.q: Why didn't “You're a genius” help Lokesh?
qa.a: It brushed past his nerves and promised something Zainab couldn't know, so it added pressure.

grounding: Shows a child learning that encouragement before a test works best with a concrete suggestion and without denying nervousness.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: Coach's note, Saturday. Gopika, under-eleven hockey. Before the penalty shoot-out, our goalkeeper, Nisha, was pale and shaking. I was about to go over when I saw Jeevan get there first. I heard him say, “It's okay to be scared. I would be.” Then: “Watch their stick, not their eyes. You saved three like that on Thursday.” Nisha nodded, and her shoulders came down. She saved two out of five. We still lost, but she walked off the pitch with her head up. I told Jeevan afterwards that what he did was real encouragement: he didn't pretend she wasn't scared, and he gave her something to do. I'd like him to help me coach the younger ones.

qa.q: How many penalties did Nisha save?
qa.a: Nisha saved two out of five.

qa.q: What was Nisha feeling before the shoot-out?
qa.a: Nisha was scared and anxious, pale and shaking.

qa.q: What made Jeevan's encouragement effective?
qa.a: He accepted that she was scared and gave a concrete tip, to watch the stick, reminding her of the three she saved on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Gopika see what Jeevan did?
qa.a: Gopika saw it as real encouragement and wanted him to help coach the younger players.

grounding: Shows a child encouraging a teammate before a challenge by accepting her fear and giving a concrete suggestion.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage:
Sunday

Samir's first swimming race today. By the pool his hands were shaking and he kept saying he felt sick. I said, "You can do it! Don't be scared!" He snapped, "I AM scared, okay?" Oops.

So I tried again. "Okay, you're nervous. That's normal. Remember what Coach says: count your strokes to the wall, like in practice. Just the counting." He nodded and started muttering "one, two, three" under his breath.

He came third! Afterwards he said the counting was the only thing in his head, and that it helped more than "you can do it". I'm going to remember that for my own exams.

Dhruv

qa.q: What place did Samir come in the race?
qa.a: Third.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when Samir snapped, "I AM scared, okay?"
qa.a: A bit embarrassed and sorry ("Oops"), realising that "Don't be scared" had brushed aside Samir's real, nervous feelings.

qa.q: What made Dhruv's second try more helpful?
qa.a: Dhruv accepted the nerves as normal and gave a concrete step: count the strokes to the wall, like in practice 👍

qa.q: How did Samir see the two kinds of encouragement afterwards?
qa.a: Samir said the counting helped more than "you can do it", because it gave his mind one thing to hold on to.

grounding: It is a child's diary about encouraging a nervous friend before a race, learning that acknowledging the nerves and giving a concrete step helps most.
